Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
Wildlife Management Unit 528 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2018-19) 
 
Background 
Buffalo Head Hills Wildlife Management Unit (WMU 528) covers an area of 12,034 km2 and is located northeast 
of Manning, Alberta. The unit is bounded to the west by the Peace River, and to the south by the 24 th baseline. 
Starting at the 24th baseline, Highway 88 forms the eastern boundary of the unit until it intersects the Bear River 
to the north. The Bear River forms the northern boundary along with the northern edge of township 103 (starting 
at range 15). 
 
While there are no major population centers within the WMU, both Manning (to the southwest) and Fort 
Vermilion (to the north) are relatively close by. The Tall Cree First Nation has two reserves along the 
northeastern boundary of the WMU, and the Paddle Prairie Metis settlement borders the northwest corner. The 
Peace, Buffalo and Wolverine River valleys provide extensive critical habitat for ungulates in the western half of 
the WMU.  
 
The unit is predominantly forested (approximately 80%), with pockets of grassland, shrubland, and burns 
interspersed throughout. Cultivated land covers a relatively small portion of the WMU (approximately 2%) and 
mostly occurs in the north. Cut blocks (at various stages of regeneration) cover approximately 5% of the land 
base. Forest harvesting and petroleum extraction are the most common land uses, and their associated 
footprints (cut blocks, roads, well pads, seismic lines, pipelines, and cutlines) occur throughout the unit.  
 
The objective of the 2019 aerial ungulate survey was to assess the status of the  moose population in WMU 528 
by estimating abundance, density and the age-sex composition. 
 
Survey Method 
An aerial survey for ungulates was conducted February 5 to 8, 2019 using distance sampling techniques 
(Buckland et al., 2001; Thomas et al., 2010). A total of 187 north-south transect lines (survey effort = 1,755 km) 
were flown with two jet ranger helicopters, each outfitted with rear bubble windows to maximize visibility . Moose 
were classified by age class (adult or juvenile) and sex. Other incidental wildlife sightings were also recorded. 
 
Results 
Moose 
A total of 143 moose were observed in 87 groups, which included 73 cows, 29 calves, 40 bulls (23 antlerless, 
17 antlered), and one unclassified individual. The estimated density was 0.104 moose/km2 (90% CI 0.081 – 
0.135) and the estimated abundance was 1,249 individuals (90% CI 966 – 1,613; Table 1). A total of 142 moose 
were successfully classified and the bull:cow:calf ratio was estimated to be 55:100:40.
